content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a safe imitation learning algorithm, LGAIL. 
The goal of safe imitation learning is to handle cases where some experts violate cost limits.
To do this, LGAIL considers constrained optimization problem and uses Lagrangian to handle constraints.
Finally, theoretical analysis and empirical results to support the proposed method are presented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

- There is a theoretical analysis of performance convergence.
- Extensive experiments are provided.

**Weakness**

- Assumption 1 does not make sense. I believe that the ‘expert’ should be experts with the exact safety constraints, not experts with the wrong safety constraints. Why are experts with wrong safety constraints called ‘experts’? Indeed, I think the suggested problem setting is not convincing.
- Can Theorem 1 guarantee the safety and performance of LGAIL? If possible, it would be nice to provide corollaries that guarantee the convergence of safety and performance, respectively.
- What is the main challenge in applying Lagrangian to GAIL? LGAIL seems to be composed of GAIL + Lagrangian without much difficulty. Especially, $\min_\lambda$ can be easily added to the existing minimization process (i.e. $\min_\alpha$).
- In table 1, looking at the mean $\pm$ variance of the cost, LGAIL seems to violate the cost limit more than RAIL. In that sense, I think RAIL is a safer offline imitation learning algorithm.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose the problem of safe generative adversarial imitation learning for which the goal is to lean a policy that mimic the expert data as well as satisfying safety constraints (that even the expert may fail to satisfy).cThey proposed the Lagrangian Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (LGAIL) algorithm that optimizes the dual GAIL occupation measure matching objective as well as a Lagrange formulation of the safety constraint. The proposed algorithm updates the Lagrange multiplier according to the level of constraint satisfaction. On top of theoretical guarantees (that is based on strong duality, similar to GAIL) empirically they show experiments in which LGAIL learns policies that matches expert's performance and at the same time satisfies safety constraints.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The problem of enforcing safety in imitation learning is important and has real-world applications in robotics and autonomous driving etc. The problem is generally challenging. 
The algorithm proposed,  while is generally an extension of the famous GAIL algorithm, is novel.
Experiments show that the proposed LGAIL algorithm achieves both safety guarantees and performance matching with expert.

Weaknesses:
Paper writing, especially the theoretical part, requires much more work to make it readable to the general ML audience. 
The safety guarantees is quite weak as it only relies on the KKT condition which guarantees safety only upon convergence. In real-life, with complex function approximation, this is never the case. The proof also relies on strong duality (similar to GAIL) but it is unclear whether with the additional safety constraints, will strong duality hold in general. If so, then the theoretical claim of this work is rather weak.
New data is needed to be collected during training and since safety is not guaranteed during training the algorithm may not be safe in execution for data collection.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In terms of novelty, this work studies a new problem of enforcing safety while imitating expert's behaviors. This is an interesting problem (of learning expert's actions while modifying that to suit the safety purpose) that has realistic applications. The paper is reasonably written and most concepts are explained. However the theoretical section can be quite hard to follow with too many notations and concepts that require better explanations. Perhaps more technical materials should be moved to appendix to make more space for better outlining the important concepts. It would also be more clear if more intuitive explanations are added to the main paper. Theorem 1's claim seems plausible though I haven't really checked the validity of the proofs. 

Hyper-parameters are included in the appendix that helps readers to reproduce the results, codes are not included.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper proposes a new problem setting in imitation learning and a simple algorithm based on extending GAIL with a Lagrangian-based approach to incorporate constraints. Novelty wise besides the new problem setting it seems the proposed algorithms (while with some form of theoretical guarantees that are similar to GAIL) are quite straight-forward. 

The experimental results illustrates the benefits of the algorithm in terms of enforcing safety as well as mimicking expert's performance.  However, more SOTA comparisons (since there's a lack of full theoretical studies on safety guarantees) are needed to support the authors' claim on the benefits of the new algorithm.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new problem setting for safe imitation learning, in which the goal is to learn policies that produce expert-like behavior but satisfy a prescribed safety constraint that’s more strict than those of experts. The authors introduce an algorithm under this problem setting called Lagrangian Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (LGAIL) that optimizes an objective that augments GAIL with a Lagrange multiplier. This algorithm dynamically tunes the weight of safety violations in order to satisfy the safety constraint. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the algorithm and safety of the learned policy. Furthermore, promising experiments results are shown on simulated control tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The problem setting is interesting and relevant in practice – in practice, sometimes we hold robots to higher safety standards compared to human experts. Although the components of the algorithms are not new, including GAIL and Lagrangian multipliers, the proposed algorithm that combines them seems novel. In addition, the experimental results of the proposed algorithm seem promising. 

However, the safety guarantees of the algorithm are weak and thus may not have much practical impact. 
- During training, it requires interaction in the real world and it’s not guaranteed that the safety constraint can be satisfied because exploration is still required. In the autonomous driving application which the authors refer to multiple times in the text, this implies potential collision during training. 
- The safety guarantee of the final policy is based on the KKT condition, which I believe holds when there’s strong duality. But it’s unclear whether the Lagrangian in Eq (4) has strong duality. 

Furthermore, it seems that the main benefit of the algorithm is being able to tune the weight parameter lambda dynamics. However, there’s only one parameter. It’s unclear whether a coarse search of the safety cost weight parameter tuning in RAIL would produce comparable performance. 

Other questions
- Are the proposed method and theory limited to tabular setting (Section 3)?
- GAIL is derived from the composition between RL and IRL operations. I wonder whether the new objective has similar interpretations. Probably learning the “reward” using IRL and solving a constraint RL problem?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has high clarity. Quality and novelty have been discussed in the previous question.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem setting and algorithm are inspiring. However, the proposed algorithm lacks strong safety guarantees and the objective considered (i.e. 1 dynamically tuned parameter) is not very challenging.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper considers the problem of safe generative imitation learning for cases wherein the goal is to learn a controller than satisfies a safety specification given some expert data. The authors consider a setting in which the learner only has access to rollouts from an expert controller collected offline. Building on GAIL, they use the Lagrangian formalism to introduce safety constraints based on CMDPs. They present LGAIL that updates the Lagrangian and the Lagrange multiplier to arrive at a safe imitator, and then empirically evaluated on safety Gym tasks. The results indicate that LGAIL can learn close-to-expert policies while satisfying safety constraints.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength

**Interesting problem.** I think this paper tackles an important and interesting problem. Imitation learning + safety is indeed suitable for many real problems, which is still relatively an open problem.

**Promising approach.** This paper presents a simple and sound method to solve the problem based on GAIL and Lagrangian relaxation.

**Experiment.** This paper presents nice experimental results compared with well-known baselines and recent one (i.e., RAIL).

### Weakness
**Paper writing.** Especially, related work section should be improved. In the paragraph entitled "Safe Reinforcement Learning", there is no argument regarding safe model-based RL, safe exploration, and formal method. I know the authors want to discuss particularly related work, but still this paragraph might provide the readers with wrong information. Also, I don't think it is a right to say that there are direct and indirect approaches for CMDPs. In the whole paper, the knowledge is not provided in an organized manner, I feel each information is just listed.

**Theoretical analysis.** In the section 4.3, total 6 assumptions are made, but it is not clear why such each is assumed or whether each assumption is natural. This is related to the above comment (in **Paper writing**), this paper is hard to follow since sentences or paragraphs are not connected with each other. In addition, Theorem 1 provides a theorem on convergence, but this is on $g(\theta_t)$. I am not sure whether this theorem guarantees that the whole algorithm (i.e., LGAIL) converges.


### Minor comments
- We denote the minimum safety constraint --> We denote the minimum safety threshold. $d$ is not a constraint.

### Quesions
[Q1] Could you tell me the thoughts about my understanding on Theorem 1?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
I think this paper is hard to follow (especially related work and theoretical analyses). Clarity should be improved by adding more intuitive explanations and pay more attention to the connections between sentences and paragraphs.

### Quality
The quality of the theoretical analyses are still dubious. I'm not fully convinced whether Theorem 1 actually guarantees the convergence of the whole algorithm under natural assumptions.

### Novelty
The problem is new; thus the proposed algorithm is also new though the algorithm itself is simple.

### Reproducibility
The source code is not attached, but I trust the authors' statement ``Our codes and data will be released upon publication.''
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper has several merits regarding 1) new problem formulation, 2) simple yet sound algorithms, and 3) promising experimental results. On the other hand, there are several issues or concerns on paper writing or theoretical analysis. Thus, I slightly lean on rejection for now.

content.title: Prescribed Safety Performance Imitation Learning from A Single Expert Dataset
content.abstract: Existing safe imitation learning (safe IL) methods mainly focus on learning safe policies that are similar to expert ones, but may fail in applications requiring different safety constraints. In this paper, we propose the Lagrangian Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (LGAIL) algorithm, which can adaptively learn safe policies from a single expert dataset under diverse prescribed safety constraints. To achieve this, we augment GAIL with safety constraints and then relax it as an unconstrained optimization problem by utilizing a Lagrange multiplier. The Lagrange multiplier enables explicit consideration of the safety and is dynamically adjusted to balance the imitation and safety performance during training. Then, we apply a two-stage optimization framework to solve LGAIL: (1) a discriminator is optimized to measure the similarity between the agent-generated data and the expert ones; (2) forward reinforcement learning is employed to improve the similarity while considering safety concerns enabled by a Lagrange multiplier. Furthermore, theoretical analyses on the convergence and safety of LGAIL demonstrate its capability of adaptively learning a safe policy given prescribed safety constraints. At last, extensive experiments in OpenAI Safety Gym conclude the effectiveness of our approach.
